name: Rose Color
lede: Rose color is a saturated pink-red, and before it was a swatch the phrase described the soft red of madder and safflower preparations.

sections.title: The color of a rose, in the trade
sections.body:
The *Pigment Compendium* shows how painters' suppliers used the phrase [1][2]. Field (1835) sold a concentrated tincture of madder of a perfect "rose colour" and transparency, under the names liquid rubiate and liquid madder lake, and Salter (1869) adds rose rubiate [1]. Alston, writing about 1804, says safflower prepared in saucers gave a rose color [2]. The compendium notes that safflower and saffron were often confused in this period [2].

So rose color was a description of tone before it was a fixed name: a transparent pinkish red from a dyestuff [1][2]. See [[irresistible]] for the dye plant behind most of it.

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch #EA598F comes from Ridgway's *Color Standards* of 1912, plate XII, hue 71, and the ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955, which sets it in the deep purplish pink block [3]. It is a bluer, more saturated pink than the madder rose of the paint trade [1][3]. Close names are [[rose]], [[rose-pink]] and [[cerise]] [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our archive of 23,781 has this color covering even 1% of its canvas, as photographed [4]. A bright pink like this is mostly a flower or fabric color, and a rare one on varnished panels and canvases [4].
